TABLE OF CONTENTS
WYOMING ATTORNEY GENERAL FORMAL OPINIONS – 1998
98-001
Who is the custodian of reports of investigations conducted by
the Office of the Attorney General, Division of Criminal
Investigation?
What considerations and procedures must be followed when a
request is made to release such reports to the general public?
Specifically, should the report of the recent investigation
conducted by the Division of Criminal Investigation, regarding
the Wyoming Office of State Lands and Investments be released
as requested?
98-002
What is the legal effect of a state agency accepting a bid by a
vehicle dealer who is not franchised to sell the particular vehicle
offered?
98-003
Does the Wyoming Legislature's use of state funds to employ a
chaplain to open daily sessions of each house with prayer violate
the United States or Wyoming constitutions?
98-004
Is the Wyoming Community College Commission legally entitled
to access to the community college system data stored on the
Administrative Computing System?

98-005
Does the leasing of prison facilities from a private entity, as
authorized by 1998 House Bill No. 0054 and 1997 Session Laws
of Wyoming, Chapter 94, § 3, create a state obligation in
violation of Wyoming's constitutional debt limitations?
98-006
Does the definition of gift under the Ethics and Disclosure Act
include food and beverages provided at receptions hosted by
various groups during legislative sessions?
Does the definition of gift under the Ethics and Disclosure Act
include incidental meals that a legislator or public official has
with a constituent or lobbyist throughout the year?
98-007
May non-residents lawfully be appointed to the positions of
assistant adjutant general of the Wyoming Air National Guard or
the Wyoming Army National Guard under Art. 6, § 15 of the
Wyoming Constitution?
98-008
Under the Ethics and Disclosure Act, WYO. STAT. 9-13-101, et
seq., is it lawful for a legislator to accept a reduced rate from a
motel for an extended stay?
If so, must other persons who are similarly situated and stay a
similar length of time (such as lobbyists) also be able to receive
the same reduced rate as legislators?
If a legislator does not stay in a motel offering reduced rates
during the legislative session, can he still accept the reduced
legislative rate during the interim between sessions when he is
on official business?
98-009

By prohibiting an elected official from supervising or managing a
family member employed in a public office or position, does
WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) effectively prohibit an elected
official's family member from working in the office of the elected official?

January 13, 1998
OPINION NO. 98-001
TO: Honorable Jim Geringer
Governor, State of Wyoming
FROM: William U. Hill
Attorney General
Matthew J. Fermelia
Senior Assistant Attorney General
Bryan Skoric
Assistant Attorney General
QUESTION NO. 1: Who is the custodian of reports of investigations conducted by the Office of the
Attorney General, Division of Criminal Investigation?
ANSWER: The custodians of such reports are the Director of Division of Criminal
Investigation, and the Attorney General.
QUESTION NO. 2: What considerations and procedures must be followed when a request is made
to release such reports to the general public?
ANSWER: Upon receipt of a formal request to release public records, the custodian
must follow those directives found in the Wyoming Public Records Act
and related caselaw authority.
QUESTION NO. 3: Specifically, should the report of the recent investigation conducted by the Division
of Criminal Investigation, regarding the Wyoming Office of State Lands and
Investments be released as requested?
ANSWER: No. While investigative reports are afforded discretionary protection,
which is a factor to be weighed, in this case it is mandatory that the report
be held in confidence, as it is deemed to be a protected, personnel record.
1

DISCUSSION
Background
In early 1997, the 54th Wyoming state legislature made changes to those state statutes concerning
the Office of State Lands and Investments (“OSLI”), formerly the State Land and Farm Loan Office, and,
in part, directed that the official rules of the OSLI be amended. Therefore, after legislative session
concluded, the OSLI began its rule change process as directed.
On July 10, 1997, the Board of Land Commissioners met to discuss and approve the proposed
new rules of the OSLI. Present at this meeting were Governor Geringer, Secretary of State Ohman, State
Auditor Ferrari, and Treasurer Smith. Superintendent of Public Instruction Catchpole was not present at
this meeting. It also became necessary for Treasurer Smith to leave the meeting early. After discussion
during this meeting, Governor Geringer called for a motion on the new, proposed rules of the OSLI.
However, no motion was made and the matter was tabled.
On July 17, 1997, another meeting of the Board of Land Commissioners was held with all members
present and the proposed rules of the OSLI were accepted and approved. These rules were then
published for public comment.
On September 5, 1997, it was learned that a change to the rules of the OSLI, as reviewed and
approved by the Board on July 17, 1997, had been made with respect to the definition of "established
roads," found in Chapter 13 of those rules. The Board of Land Commissioners had not approved this
change and its members were unaware that such a change had been made.
Upon initial inquiry, it was suggested by the Director of OSLI that someone had gained
unauthorized access to the OSLI office and its computer system, either physically or electronically, and had
made the change in question as a result of that unauthorized entry. This suggestion was subsequently
echoed by the Deputy Director of OSLI. Concerned with the possible criminal implications of such a
scenario, the Governor requested the assistance of the Office of the Attorney General, Division of Criminal
investigation ("DCI"), which began its investigation on September 12, 1997.
During the investigation of these above events by the DCI, it was discovered that the change in
question was made during business hours on July 15, 1997, in the offices of the OSLI, by an employee of
that agency. Upon completion of its investigation, DCI prepared a investigative report which was then
given to the Laramie County District Attorney for his analysis, and to Governor Geringer, as Chairman of
the Board of Land Commissioners. Upon the Governor's review of the DCI report, and based in part upon
its findings, the Governor removed James H. Magagna from his position of Director at the OSLI effective
November 25, 1997. Deputy Director Steve Degenfelder also tendered his resignation effective that same
date. In addition, a formal personnel investigation was opened concerning employees in the OSLI who
2

were, or who may have been, knowledgeable regarding the rules change.
Subsequently, the Office of the Governor, the Office of Attorney General and the Division of
Criminal Investigation each received a formal public records request from a reporter of the Wyoming
Tribune-Eagle requesting release of the above referenced DCI report. In addition, the Office of the
Attorney General later received a written request from a reporter of the Casper Star Tribune, also
requesting that the DCI report be released. The Office of the Governor then requested an opinion of the
Office of Attorney General to respond to the questions posed herein.
3

QUESTION NO. 1
The Wyoming Public Records Act found at WYO. STAT. § 16-4-201 et seq. details the process
to be followed when the release of public records is requested and when denial of such a request is
believed to be appropriate. As media requests have gone to different State officials the threshold question
must be, who is the custodian of the requested DCI report?
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-201 defines who shall be considered the custodian or official custodian of
such public records. In applicable part, that section states as follows:
(a) As used in this act:
(i)"Custodian" means the official custodian or any authorized person having
personal custody and control of the public records in question;
(ii)"Official custodian" means any officer or employee of the state or any
agency, institution or political subdivision thereof, who is responsible for
the maintenance, care and keeping of public records, regardless of
whether the records are in his actual personal custody and control;
No Wyoming caselaw authority exists which further defines these terms as used in this act. In
interpreting the definitions, one must review the plain meaning of the words used in such definitions, along
with the intent of the lawmakers who adopted the law. It is axiomatic in Wyoming that this is the
appropriate rule of interpretation to be followed. An excellent discussion of the subject can be found in
Parker Land & Cattle v. Wyo. Game & Fish, 845 P.2d 1040, 1042-1043 (Wyo. 1993).
Looking at the definition of "custodian," and the ordinary and obvious, words used therein, it is clear
that a custodian for purposes of the act shall mean the official custodian as subsequently defined therein or
any authorized person having personal custody and control of the public records in question. In this
instance, the Director of the DCI and/or the Attorney General are the authorized persons having personal
custody and control of written reports of investigations performed by the DCI. Thus, it appears that these
two persons are the "custodians" of such reports as defined in the act, with the Attorney General having
ultimate authority, as the head of the agency.
Upon review of the definition of "official custodian," a similar conclusion must be reached. It is
equally clear that the Director of the DCI and/or the Attorney General act as the designated officers of the
DCI and its overseeing state office, the Office of Attorney General, and are responsible for the care and
safekeeping of written reports of the investigations performed by the DCI. Additionally, these persons
possess supervisory authority over any other employee within the DCI or Office of Attorney General who
may on a day-to-day basis be responsible for the care and safekeeping of these records.
4

Finally, while no legislative history exists with respect to the act, a review of the law as a whole
supports this interpretation. It is common sense that the legislature would have intended that the persons
to have decision making authority regarding public records would be those same persons in positions of
authority, having both personal custody and control over public records and responsibility for their care and
safekeeping within the agency or department from which the public records were derived. In fact, the
statute does not allow any other reasonable interpretation of the definitions of "custodian" and "official
custodian”. It must be concluded that both the custodians and official custodians of written reports of
investigations prepared by the DCI would be the Director of the DCI and/or the Attorney General.
QUESTION NO. 2
The Wyoming Public Records Act outlines when reports and records of the State of Wyoming may
be released to the general public. Specifically, WYO. STAT. § 16-4-202(a) provides as follows:
(a) All public records shall be open for inspection by any person at
reasonable times, except as provided in this act or as otherwise
provided by law, but the official custodian of any public records
may make rules and regulations with reference to the inspection
of the records as is reasonably necessary for the protection of the
records and the prevention of unnecessary interference with the
regular discharge of the duties of this custodian or his office.
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203 is of particular importance in this case. In subsection(a), the legislature
begins to list the exceptions to the general rule regarding disclosure. A custodian of a public record may
deny the inspection of records or any portion of such records if the inspection 1) will be contrary to any
state statute, 2) the inspection would be contrary to federal statute or regulation issued thereunder having
the force and effect of law, or 3) the inspection is prohibited by rules promulgated by the Supreme Court
or by the order of any court of record.
Subsection (b) sets forth categories of records the release of which is subject to the discretion of
the custodian. In these cases a custodian may deny the right of inspection of certain records on the grounds
that disclosure of such records would be contrary to the public interest. Included within these discretionary
exceptions are “. . .(i) Records of investigations conducted by . . . the attorney general . . . or any
investigatory file compiled for any other law enforcement or prosecution purposes."
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(d) sets forth instances in which the inspection of records must be
denied, unless otherwise provided by law,
" . . .(d) The custodian shall deny the right of inspection of the following records . . . .” Included in this
category are elements of personnel files,
. . . (iii) Personnel files except those files shall be available to the duly elected and appointed officials
who supervise the work of the person in interest. Applications, performance ratings and scholastic
5

achievement data shall be available only to the person in interest and to the duly elected and appointed
officials who supervise his work . . . .”
In Sheridan Newspapers, Inc. v. City of Sheridan, 660 P.2d 785 (Wyo. 1983), which involved
the discretionary withdrawal of routine police records from public scrutiny, the Wyoming Supreme Court
thoroughly discusses the degree of review and the process to be applied when a formal request for release
of public records is received. The Court acknowledges a presumption that public records should be
disclosed to the general public, but articulates as well that, in certain instances, a custodian of certain
categories of records may deny their release if there is a legal basis for non-disclosure.
The Court goes on to direct that when a demand to release public records is made, the custodian
of records possessing such discretionary authority must weigh the competing interests involved and
determine whether publication would result in harm to the public interest, which would outweigh the
legislative policy favoring the release of eligible records. If the custodian decides against release, he must
state specific public policy reasons for the refusal. These reasons then are available for review by a court,
if necessary. See WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(e) and (f).
Although the facts of the referenced case differ from those before us, certainly we may take
direction from the opinion as to the discretionary withdrawal of certain categories of records from public
view. In summary, if a formal request is made for the release of public records which are subject to
discretionary withdrawal by their custodian, a determination must be made by the custodian if the records
should be disclosed or if, within the discretion of such custodian, sufficient reasons exist for the denial of
the request. Specifically, in order for the custodian of a public record to effectuate withdrawal of a public
record under the Act, he must: 1) determine whether the individual record in question falls within statutory
exemptions provided under the Act; 2) if so, weigh the competing interest involving the public's right to
know against the perceived harm to the public from disclosure; and finally; 3) if he chooses to withdraw
records from public inspection, he must provide reasons for doing so. Thereafter, in the event of a court
action, the custodian must satisfy the court that statutory withdrawal, in light of the public interest, outweighs
the public policy favoring disclosure.
QUESTION NO. 3
In the instant case, the custodians of the DCI report on the OSLI investigation are the Director of
the DCI and the Attorney General. It is their responsibility to respond to the pending requests. As
custodians, they must make all necessary determinations with respect to the requested release of the DCI
report in compliance with the Public Records Act and applicable caselaw.
Upon careful review of the factual scenario and application of the Public Records Act and caselaw,
we conclude that sufficient and substantial reasons exist for these custodians to deny the release of the DCI
report regarding the OSLI investigation.
6

As noted previously, pursuant to WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(b)(i) the right of inspection of records
of investigations conducted by the attorney general may be denied on the ground that disclosure would be
contrary to the public interest. That discretionary denial clearly is available in this instance.
For example, during the OSLI investigation conducted by the DCI, it was necessary for the DCI
to conduct numerous interviews. Public disclosure of the identity of those interviewed and the information
they provided to the DCI investigators would be a hindrance to future DCI investigations. Since it is not
common practice for investigative reports of the DCI to be made public, individuals in future investigations
may be less than forthright or unwilling to be interviewed at all, believing that their identity and statements
will be made public. It is surely within the public interest to protect the investigative process with respect
to DCI investigations, and the law appropriately gives the custodian the right to deny the inspection of both
investigatory reports and those reports compiled for prosecution purposes. As DCI conducts only
investigations into possible criminal activity, the report in question qualifies on both counts, no less so even
though prosecution ultimately was declined.
A second strong argument supports the denial of the pending requests. Also as noted previously,
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(d)(iii) mandates the confidentiality of certain elements of personnel files,
including things as seemingly benign as applications, school records and performance ratings.
The contents of the DCI report in question were cited as the basis, at least in part, for the dismissal
of the Director of the OSLI and the resignation of his Deputy. Furthermore, the report concerning the
OSLI prompted the opening of a formal, personnel investigation concerning employees within the OSLI.
Accordingly, this report is deemed to be a part of each of these respective employees' personnel files. As
personnel and disciplinary actions are involved, clearly performance is implicated. There can be no choice,
no exercise of discretion as to the DCI report. As it is deemed to be a protected part of personnel records
the request for public inspection must be denied.
It should be noted that the employment status of an employee of the State of Wyoming is of no
consequence to this discussion. The mandatory protection afforded personnel files by the Public Records
Act does not distinguish between the files of classes of employees whatsoever, be they permanent, at will,
contract or any other variety.
It should also be noted that the Public Records Act provides a simple remedy to disappointed
applicants seeking the release of public records. That remedy may be found at WYO. STAT. § 16-4-
203(f) which states:
(f) A person denied the right to inspect any record covered by this act
may apply to the district court of the district wherein the record is found
for any order directing the custodian of the record to show cause why he
should not permit the inspection of the record.
7

It is a foregone conclusion that there are those who will be critical of this analysis of the Public
Records Act. They may suggest that this application of its provisions is too narrow or something more
dramatic. If so, then by all means they should avail themselves of the remedy just noted and present their
arguments to a court. But there is no mystery to this opinion. The law says what it says. And if the
interpretation offered here should be held to be erroneous, it is far preferable to be told by a court that a
record must be released, than to be told by a court that by releasing a critical element of a personnel file,
in contravention of state law, the State has civilly injured a former employee and is now liable for damages.
In this case, the State must weigh statutory language that prohibits the release of certain personnel
records, the integrity and effectiveness of DCI investigations and the realities of the explosion in
employment litigation which continues to drain more and more State resources, against media curiosity.
Given these circumstances prudence dictates caution. Accordingly, until or unless a court orders the
release of the report in question, it is deemed to be a protected part of personnel files, as contemplated by
the Wyoming Public Records Act, and it will not be released or made available for inspection.
CONCLUSION
The custodians of reports of investigations performed by the DCI are the Director of the DCI
and/or the Attorney General. A determination with respect to the release of such public records must be
made by those custodians with regard to the Public Records Act and applicable caselaw authority. Finally,
the media requests will be denied based upon the exceptions afforded investigative and personnel files in
the Wyoming Public Records Act.
8

QUESTION: What is the legal effect of a state agency accepting a bid by a vehicle dealer who is not
franchised to sell the particular vehicle offered?
ANSWER: See Discussion.
DISCUSSION
This office is advised that some agencies have attempted to acquire motor vehicles through the
competitive bidding process and accordingly have issued a request for proposal to various car dealers.
Further, we are advised that in some cases, a dealer who had the lowest bid was not franchised or
licensed to sell the type of motor vehicle he was offering to the agency. Other car dealers complained
about this circumstance, and this office has been asked for advice as to the legal consequences of such
a transaction.
The Wyoming Motor Vehicle Franchise Act, WYO. STAT. §§ 31-16-101 through 31-16-124
is very specific as to the qualifications of vehicle dealers to offer to sell or sell particular motor vehicles.
9

In particular, WYO. STAT. § 31-16-108 sets forth "Unlawful acts" and partially provides:
(a) No person required to be licensed under this act shall:
* * *
(x) Display for sale, exchange or sell any new motor vehicle for which
the vehicle dealer does not hold a valid franchise; (emphasis added)
A franchise is defined in WYO. STAT. § 31-16-101(a)(x) as:
. . . a contract or agreement between a vehicle dealer and a manufacturer or its
distributor or factory branch by which the dealer is authorized to engage in the business
of selling any specified make of new vehicles;... (emphasis added)
Consequently, a motor vehicle dealer must have a franchise for the particular vehicle that he is
intending to sell. If there is no franchise, then the dealer is operating in violation of the Wyoming Motor
Vehicle Franchise Act.1
The Wyoming Motor Vehicle Franchise Act prohibits a non-franchised vehicle dealer from
offering to sell or selling a particular franchised vehicle. Consequently, where the dealer has not been
enfranchised or licensed to sell the line or make of vehicles under Wyoming law, it may not legally
submit a bid.
Finally, the Wyoming Motor Vehicle Franchise Act specifically sets forth the legal effect of any
contract made in violation of its provisions. WYO. STAT. § 31-16-124(c) provides that: "Any
provision of any agreement, franchise, waiver, novation or other written instrument which is in violation
of any section of this act is null and void and without force and effect. " Thus, any state contract
consummating a purchase of a vehicle from a nonfranchised dealer would be void.
We suggest that any future bid specifications contain language that restricts bidding to
franchised dealers to avoid potential violations of the foregoing Act.
1 WYO. STAT. § 31-16-103(d), does authorize a vehicle dealer to
dispose of the stock of new vehicles which the dealer had on hand when
he lost the franchise. Thus, this dealer could submit a bid although he
does not have a current franchise.
10

QUESTION: Does the Wyoming Legislature's use of state funds to employ a chaplain to open daily
sessions of each house with prayer violate the United States or Wyoming
constitutions?1
ANSWER: No. Please see discussion.
DISCUSSION
1 Pursuant to Rules, Senate and House of Representatives, Fifty-
Fourth Wyoming Legislature, 1997-1998, the Wyoming Senate and the
Wyoming House of Representatives begin their legislative business days
with a prayer by a chaplain. See Rule 4-1 of the Rules of the Senate and
Rule 2-1 of the Rules of the House of Representatives.
11

A. United States Constitution
The first question this opinion must address is whether the Wyoming Legislature's use of public
funds to employ chaplains to open legislative sessions with prayer violates the antiestablishment
provision of the United States Constitution. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution,
made applicable to the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, provides:
Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion,
or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or
of the press; or of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the
government for redress of grievances. (emphasis added)
The United States Supreme Court has already addressed this same issue and answered the
question in the negative. In 1983, a Nebraska taxpayer challenged the constitutionality of the Nebraska
Legislature's practice of opening each legislative session with a prayer led by a state paid chaplain.
Marsh v. Chambers, 463 U.S. 783, 103 S. Ct. 3330 (1983). In holding that this practice did not
violate the United States Constitution, the Supreme Court noted:
The opening of sessions of legislative and other deliberative public
bodies with prayer is deeply embedded in the history and tradition of this
country. From colonial times through the founding of the Republic and ever
since, the practice of legislative prayer has coexisted with the principles of
disestablishment and religious freedom. In the very courtrooms in which the
United States District Judge and later three Circuit Judges heard and decided
this case, the proceedings opened with an announcement that concluded, "God
save the United States and this Honorable Court." The same invocation occurs
at all sessions of this Court.
Marsh, 103 S.Ct. at 3333.
The Supreme Court usually employs the following three part test in determining whether a
practice or law violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment:
(1) Does the practice or law have a secular purpose?
(2) Does the primary effect of the challenged practice or law neither advance nor
inhibit religion?
(3) Does the practice or law avoid excessive government entanglement with
religion?
12

Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602, 612-613, 91 S.Ct. 2105, 2111 (1971). In reviewing the
constitutionality of opening legislative sessions with prayer, however, the Supreme Court deviated from
its standard establishment analysis. It instead looked solely to the longstanding tradition of opening
legislative sessions with prayer and concluded, based upon that longstanding tradition, first, that the
framers of the United States Constitution did not intend to prohibit the practice, and second, that the
practice does not pose a real threat to the required separation of church and state. Marsh, 103 S.Ct.
at 3335.
The Court explained its reliance solely upon the long history of legislative prayer as follows:
Standing alone, historical patterns cannot justify contemporary
violations of constitutional guarantees, but there is far more here than
simply historical patterns. In this context, historical evidence sheds light
not only on what the draftsmen intended the Establishment Clause to
mean, but also on how they thought that Clause applied to the practice
authorized by the First Congress--their actions reveal their intent.
* * *
It can hardly be thought that in the same week Members of the First
Congress voted to appoint and to pay a Chaplain for each House and
also voted to approve the draft of the First Amendment for submission
to the States, they intended the Establishment Clause of the
Amendment to forbid what they had just declared acceptable. In
applying the First Amendment to the states through the Fourteenth
Amendment, it would be incongruous to interpret that clause as
imposing more stringent First Amendment limits on the States than the
draftsmen imposed on the Federal Government.
This unique history leads us to accept the interpretation of the
First Amendment draftsmen who saw no real threat to the
Establishment Clause arising from a practice of prayer similar to that
now challenged.
Marsh, 103 S.Ct. at 3335 (citations omitted).
In summarizing its opinion that opening legislative sessions with prayer does not violate the
Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, the Supreme Court wrote:
We do not doubt the sincerity of those, who like respondent,
believe that to have prayer in this context risks the beginning of the
13

establishment the Founding Fathers feared. But this concern is not well
founded, for as Justice Goldberg aptly observed in his concurring
opinion in Abington, 374 U.S. at 308, 83 S.Ct. at 1616:
"It is of course true that great consequences can grow from
small beginnings, but the measure of constitutional adjudication is the
ability and willingness to distinguish between real threat and mere
shadow."
The unbroken practice for two centuries in the National
Congress, for more than a century in Nebraska and in many other
states, gives abundant assurance that there is no real threat "while this
Court sits[.]"
Marsh, 103 S.Ct. at 3338 (citations omitted).
B. Wyoming Constitution
The second question this opinion must address is whether the Wyoming Legislature's use of
public funds to employ chaplains to open legislative sessions with prayer violates the Wyoming
Constitution. Article 1, § 19 of the Wyoming Constitution, the constitution's antiestablishment clause,
provides:
No money of the state shall ever be given or appropriated to
any sectarian or religious society or institution.
The constitutionality of using public funds to open legislative meetings with prayer has not been
addressed by the Wyoming Supreme Court, but the practice has withstood state constitutional
challenges in states with constitutional provisions similar to or more restrictive than Wyoming's
provisions. See Society of Separationists, Inc. v. Whitehead, 870 P.2d 916 (Utah 1993); Colo v.
Treasurer and Receiver General, 392 N.E.2d 1195 (Mass. 1979). The Utah and Massachusetts
courts have used different approaches in analyzing this issue, and we find guidance in both decisions.
In Whitehead, the Utah Supreme Court considered whether the Salt Lake City Council's
practice of permitting prayer during a portion of the city council's meeting violated Article 1, § 4 of the
Utah Constitution. Article 1, § 4 provides, in part:
No public money or property shall be appropriated for or applied to
any religious worship, exercise or instruction, or for the support of any
ecclesiastical establishment.
14

Whitehead, 870 P. 2d at 917.
The Utah Supreme Court did not rely upon the United States Supreme Court's analysis in
Marsh, but instead created its own test for determining whether a practice violates the Utah
antiestabhshment clause. The Utah Court concluded that what Utah's constitution prohibited is the
government conferring a direct benefit upon a particular religion, and the court defined a direct benefit
as one preferring one religion over another. An indirect benefit, and one that is therefore acceptable, is
one which meets two criteria; first, the practice, supported by public funds, must be nondiscriminatory,
and second, the government must carry out the practice in a manner which permits all religions or
secular groups an opportunity to participate in the practice. Whitehead, 870 P.2d at 937-938.
Under the Utah court's analysis, the question, in our context, can be reduced to whether the
legislature is preferring certain religions or religious beliefs over others in employing a chaplain to open
the legislative sessions with prayer. This office has not been asked to evaluate the constitutionality of a
particular opening prayer, the choosing of a particular prayer, or the specific circumstances surrounding
any instance in which either house has retained a chaplain. As a general matter, under the Utah
analysis, the Wyoming Legislature's practice is constitutional, as long as the Legislature is not preferring
one set of religious beliefs over another in choosing a chaplain to recite the opening prayer.
The Massachusetts Supreme Court took a different approach in analyzing this issue. It
employed the three part test that the United States Supreme Court usually uses in analyzing issues under
the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Colo, 392 N.E.2d at 1200. That test. outlined
earlier in this opinion, considers three questions:
(1) Does the practice or law have a secular purpose?
(2) Does the primary effect of the challenged practice or law
neither advance nor inhibit religion?
(3) Does the practice or law avoid excessive government
entanglement with religion?
Colo, 392 N.E.2d at 1200.
In concluding that the Massachusetts practice of expending public monies to pay the salaries of
legislative chaplains did not violate the Massachusetts antiestablishment provision2, the Massachusetts
2 Article 3 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, as amended
by Article 11 of the Articles of Amendment to the Massachusetts Constitution,
provides, in part:
15

Supreme Court answered the three questions as follows:
The secular purposes of opening invocations are the
maintenance of long tradition and the continuation of a ritual which
prompts legislators to reflect on the gravity and solemnity of their
responsibilities and of the acts they are about to perform. Although the
opening prayers have a religious nature, it cannot be said that their
primary effect is to advance religion. * * * [Mature legislators may

unsupervised by the State, and attendance completely voluntary. There

decisions about which religions are to be represented or what sorts of

OPINION NO. 98-004
TO: Linda Vosika, Chair
Wyoming Community College Commission
FROM: William U. Hill
Attorney General
Michael L. Hubbard
Deputy Attorney General
Rowena L. Heckert
Senior Assistant Attorney General
QUESTION: Is the Wyoming Community College Commission legally entitled to access to the
community college system data stored on the Administrative Computing System?
ANSWER: Yes.
DISCUSSION
The question presented concerns access by the Wyoming Community College Commission to
the Administrative Computing System on which the colleges store their data. Since the December 2,
1997, request for "a copy of the entire LIVE account in Tape Archiver (TAR) format on a 4 mm DAT
tape," the Commission has experienced resistance from the colleges, including, in some instances, denial
of access to their computing databases.
This resistance apparently is based upon interpretations given the Family Educational Rights and
Privacy Act (FERPA), also known as the Buckley Amendment, found at 20 U.S.C. § 1232g, and the
Wyoming Public Records Act.
18

Community College Commission Responsibilities
The Commission is required to promulgate rules which "will ensure the operation and
maintenance of the community college system in a coordinated, efficient and effective manner." WYO.
STAT. § 21-18-202(a)(ii). It has done so. The Commission is also required to:
establish and implement an effective management information system
which will provide composite data about the community colleges and
assure that special analyses and studies of the colleges are conducted,
as necessary, to provide accurate and cost-effective information about
the colleges and the community college system as a whole, including an
analysis of administrative costs per full-time equivalency at each college
and an analysis of space utilization at each college.
WYO. STAT. § 21-18-202(a)(v).
The rules provide that the Commission will have access to college district data which will be
kept secure (in accordance with FERPA) and only released in composite form. The rules also require
that the colleges will use uniform administrative computing software to facilitate system-level data
collection by the Commission. Further, the rules provide that the colleges will ensure real-time, inquiry
only, access to their administrative computing systems by the Commission for its statutory purposes.
Wyoming Community College Commission Rules, Chapter 11.
Also, the $3.989 million appropriation for the management information system for the seven
colleges and the Commission was provided to the Commission for the purchase and operation of the
computer network linking all community colleges with the Commission. 1991 Laws, ch. 258, § 200. It
was intended to enable the Commission to establish the management information system from which it
could then conduct the special analyses and studies to produce the composite data in its reports.
19

Federal Legal Requirements
Under Wyoming law, the Commission is treated as an integral part of the community college
system for administrative computing purposes. Similarly, under federal law, state educational authorities
are given access to the otherwise protected personally identifiable data without the need for consent
from the subject of the records. The most pertinent provision in the federal law states:
(5) Nothing in this section [20 U.S.C. § 1232g, FERPA] shall be
construed to prohibit State and local educational officials from having
access to student or other records which may be necessary in
connection with the audit and evaluation of any federally or State
supported education program or in connection with the enforcement of
the Federal legal requirements which relate to any such program,
subject to the conditions specified in the proviso in paragraph (3).
[keep it confidential and destroy it when no longer needed] (emphasis
added)
20 U.S.C. § 1232g(b). The federal regulations contain essentially the same language. 34 C.F.R. §§
99.31(a)(3)(iii) and 99.35.
In addition, the federal law, at 20 U.S.C. § 1232g(b)(1), provides that no funds shall be
available to any educational institution which has a policy or practice of permitting the release of
education records of students without consent, other than to the following:
***
(C) authorized representatives of . . . State educational authorities
under the conditions set forth in paragraph (3) of this subsection;
(F) organizations [including state agencies] conducting studies for, or on
behalf of, educational agencies or institutions for the purpose of
developing, validating, or administering predictive tests, administering
student aid programs, and improving instruction, if such studies are
conducted in such a manner as will not permit the personal identification
of students and their parents by persons other than representatives of
such organizations and such information will be destroyed when no
longer needed for the purpose for which it is conducted; (emphasis
added)
The federal regulations define "organizations" as used in (F) above as including state agencies.
34 C.F.R. § 99.31(a)(6)(iii). Paragraph (F) addresses a major role of the Commission concerning the
community college system. It is, of course, to improve instruction and programs and ensure a
20

"coordinated, efficient, and effective" community college system. WYO. STAT. § 21-18-202. The
commission administers the State Student Incentive Grant, a federal matching student aid program
which assisted approximately four hundred students last year. The Commission also continually works
toward improving instruction throughout the system.
The references above to "paragraph (3)" refer to release of educational records to State
educational authorities when the records "may be necessary in connection with the audit and evaluation
of Federally-supported education programs, or in connection with the enforcement of the Federal legal
requirements which relate to such programs." It includes the proviso that the State authorities must
protect the confidentiality of the information and destroy it when no longer needed for the audit,
evaluation, and enforcement of the federal legal requirements. 20 U.S.C. § 1232g(b)(3).
In view of the many statutorily authorized purposes for which the Commission needs full access
to the information on the computing system, it is our view that the Family Educational Rights and
Privacy Act is no impediment to the Commission's exercising full access to the community college
system database.
The Commission is, of course, bound by the above quoted law in its
handling and ultimately its destruction of the data. For the "audit and evaluation" of educational
programs, for the administration of student aid programs, for studies for the improvement of instruction,
and for all other reports to be issued by the Commission, no personally identifiable information may be
disclosed.
21

The Wyoming Public Records Act
Turning to the Wyoming Public Records Act, there appears to be no additional protection for
community college student records. There is protection from disclosure for:
Personnel files except those shall be available to the duly elected and
appointed officials who supervise the work of the person in interest.
Applications, performance ratings and scholastic achievement data shall
be available only to the person in interest and to the duly elected and
appointed officials who supervise his work.
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(d)(iii). The Commission has no need for the applications, performance
ratings, and scholastic achievement of the employees of the community colleges. There is also no
reason, which we can discern, why such data would be entered into the system database and therefore
potentially available to many staff members within the college.
That section of the law goes on to state:
Employment contracts, working agreements or other documents setting
forth the terms and conditions of employment of public officials and
employees are not considered part of a personnel file and shall be
available for public inspection;
WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(d)(iii).
In construing this law, a court would give the ordinary and obvious meaning to the words,
consider all related statutes together, and give effect to every word, clause, and sentence. Houghton
v. Franscell, 870 P.2d 1050, 1053 (Wyo. 1994). A court would also look to the mischief the act was
intended to cure and the public policy of the state, among other things, to determine the legislative intent
of a statute.
The Wyoming Supreme Court has interpreted the Public Records Act on numerous occasions.
It has held:
The object of the public records act is disclosure, not secrecy, and we
therefore interpret the act liberally in favor of disclosure, construing all
exemptions narrowly. [citations omitted] Legislation requiring disclosure
of information is considered remedial and
[r]emedial statutes are liberally construed to suppress
the evil and advance the remedy. The policy that a
remedial statute should be liberally construed in order
22

to effectuate the remedial purpose for which it was
enacted is firmly established.
The remedial purpose of the public records act is to permit access to
public records unless disclosure would inflict irreparable harm contrary
to protected rights. (emphasis added)
Houghton v. Franscell, supra, at 1052.
In another decision, the Wyoming Supreme Court has held that public officials may not:
deny inspection of individual or classes of documents... simply because
some exempt material may be included in those records. ... [They also
may not withdraw a particular record] where it is possible for the
sensitive information to be excised and the balance of the record made
available to public inspection. Exempt material can be segregated. The
records may be structured to provide the information the public is
entitled to have.
Sheridan Newspapers, Inc. v. City of Sheridan, 660 P.2d 785, 797 (Wyo. 1983).
The Wyoming Supreme Court has held that "[m]aintaining an open and accountable
government is particularly important with respect to the expenditure of public funds." Houghton v.
Franscell, supra, at 1052, 1056. The issue of the expenditure of public funds is at the core of the
Commission's request for data on the administrative computing system and the responsibility of the
Commission to "ensure the operation and maintenance of the community college system in a
coordinated, efficient and effective manner." WYO. STAT. § 21-18-202(a)(ii).
Access to public records is a constitutionally protected interest, such that "absent a compelling
state interest, the state may not exclude an entire class of records from public inspection." Houghton v.
Franscell, supra, at 1053. The burden of demonstrating that interest falls upon the public entity which
seeks to deny access. Sheridan Newspapers, Inc. v. City of Sheridan, supra, at 796. The
Wyoming Supreme Court went on to hold:
When [the custodian] does withdraw records, reasons therefor must be
given so that these reasons may provide grounds for review should
court action result. ... In that event, the custodian must be able to satisfy
the court that, in the balancing process, statutory withdrawal, when
viewed in the spotlight of public-interest protections, outweighs the
public policy which emphasizes disclosure. If, however, the custodian
gives either no reasons or inadequate reasons for withdrawal,
appropriate legal action is available to force an automatic disclosure of
23

the records.
Sheridan Newspapers, Inc. v. City of Sheridan, supra, at 799, quoting
Newspapers, Inc. v. Brier, 89 Wis.2d 417, 279 N.W.2d 179, 184 (1979).
The Wyoming Supreme Court has discussed this weighing process further. It has adopted
Georgia's definition of invasion of privacy for purposes of exempting records from disclosure under the
public records act. An unwarranted invasion of privacy, for purposes of exemption under the Georgia
Open Records Act, is:
unwarranted publicity, unwarranted appropriation or exploitation of
one's personality, or the publicizing of one's private affairs with which
the public had no legitimate concern.
Houghton v. Franscell, supra, at 1055, citing Richmond County Hospital Authority v.S.E.
Newspapers Corp., 252 Ga. 19, 311 S.E.2d 806, 807 (1984).
With this lengthy explanation of the meaning of the Wyoming Public Records Act, we now turn
back to the exemption apparently relied upon by the colleges in resisting access by the Commission to
their databases. First, it cannot be overemphasized that the Commission is not a news organization
bent upon releasing any personally identifiable information to the public. It is constrained in this by the
same laws as the colleges are, as well as by the language in WYO. STAT. § 21-18-202(a)(v) limiting
Commission releases to "composite data."
Next, it is abundantly clear if there is any highly sensitive data (which is lawfully exempt from
disclosure) on the system, it cannot be used to justify denying access to whole classifications of data.
Sheridan Newspapers, Inc. v. City of Sheridan, supra, at 797. If such is the case, however, one
might question the judgment of the authorities who allow such data on the system.
As stated above, there is an exemption from disclosure in the Wyoming Public Records Act for
certain kinds of personnel data: the personnel files, including applications, performance ratings, and
scholastic achievement data. WYO. STAT. § 16-4-203(d)(iii). These exemptions must be narrowly
construed, and they apply to information that the Commission is not seeking. However, the
employment records on the system should be available to the Commission. If they are presently mixed
with data exempt from disclosure, the burden is on the colleges to separate them. Id.
Other concerns that were raised include the embarrassment that might ensue from disclosing
that staff members may be subject to IRS or other garnishments and withholding of past due child
support and alimony. These matters already appear in public court files, and the proffered reasons to
deny disclosure do not rise to the level of justifying interference with the Commission's responsibilities.
These are not the kinds of records the Commission is seeking.
24

Again it must be emphasized that there will be no public disclosure of personally identifiable
information by the Commission to the public. Under such circumstances, it is difficult to postulate any
harm whatsoever to the individuals involved, and certainly no "unwarranted invasion of privacy."
25

OPINION NO. 98-005
TO: State Building Commission
FROM: William U. Hill
Attorney General
Michael L. Hubbard
Deputy Attorney General
Jennifer A. Evans
Senior Assistant Attorney General
QUESTION: Does the leasing of prison facilities from a private entity, as authorized by 1998 House
Bill No. 0054 and 1997 Session Laws of Wyoming, Chapter 94, § 3, create a state
obligation in violation of Wyoming's constitutional debt limitations?
ANSWER: No. Please see discussion.
DISCUSSION
I. Background.
In 1997, the legislature, through 1997 Wyoming Session Laws, Chapter 94, § 3, authorized the
Department of Corrections to lease prison facilities from a private entity, as an alternative to financing
the construction of the new facilities with a direct appropriation of the entire cost of the project or with
capital facilities revenue bonds issued by the state. The additional provisions of HB0054 authorize the
State Building Commission, subject to certain conditions, to approve the formation of the private entity
from which the prison facilities may be leased. Passage of HBOO54 will authorize the state to use the
following financing structure, hereinafter referred to as lease revenue financing, for construction of the
new prison facilities:
1. A nonprofit corporation will be formed under the Wyoming Nonprofit Corporation Act. The
membership of the corporation's board of directors and the corporation's formation will be
approved by the State Building Commission. The nonprofit corporation is an entity separate
from the state, entitled the Wyoming Building Corporation.
26

2. The state owns the land on which the new prison facilities are to be constructed, and the state
will lease that land to the Wyoming Building Corporation for a term of twenty-four years.
3. The Wyoming Building Corporation will issue bonds in an amount sufficient to cover the costs
of constructing the new prison facilities, and the bond proceeds will be used to construct the
new facilities.
4. The Wyoming Building Corporation will enter into a construction agreement with the state.
Under the construction agreement, the state will be responsible for the construction and
equipping of the new prison facilities for a fixed price.
5. The Wyoming Building Corporation will own the new prison facilities, and the state will lease
the facilities from the corporation for a term of nineteen years. The Wyoming Building
Corporation will use the lease payments to pay off its bond debt and to pay the costs of
providing property damage and public liability insurance and utilities and any taxes or other
governmental charges payable with respect to the prison property. The bond debt will be
serviced over a term of twenty years.
6. The state will lease the prison facilities from the Wyoming Building Corporation for a term of
nineteen years, but the lease may be terminated at any time if the legislature does not
appropriate funds for any annual rental payment. At the end of its lease term, the state may
exercise an option to purchase the prison facilities for a fixed amount that is approximately
twice the amount of the state's annual rental payment under the terms of the lease.
The state's leasing of the new prison facilities will be conditioned on the following terms, which
must be included in the lease:
• The state's full faith and credit shall not be pledged for any payments under the lease;
• The state may terminate the lease at any time, without penalty or recourse against the
state, if the legislature does not appropriate sufficient funds to pay any annual rental
payment;
• No bonds or other obligations of the lessor (the Wyoming Building Corporation) shall
constitute an obligation, legal, moral or otherwise, of the state, within the meaning of any
constitutional or statutory provision;
• The obligation of the state to make any payments due under the lease in any fiscal year
shall be limited to funds appropriated by the legislature for that fiscal year; and
• All bonds or other obligations of the lessor (Wyoming Building Corporation) relating to
27

the prison facilities shall contain disclaimers describing the limitations on the state's
obligations.
The question which has been presented is whether the Wyoming Building Corporation's bond
issue, or the state's lease of the prison facilities from the Wyoming Building Corporation, constitutes an
obligation of the state in excess of its current year's taxes, and thus violates Wyoming's constitutional
debt limitations.
II. Wyoming Law.
Article 16, § 2 of the Wyoming Constitution provides:
No debt in excess of the taxes for the current year, shall in any
manner be created in the State of Wyoming, unless the proposition to
create such debt shall have been submitted to a vote of the people and
by them approved; except to suppress insurrection or to provide for the
public defense.
Section 2 is intended to prohibit the legislature from creating long-term debt and thereby binding future
legislatures to make appropriations in future fiscal years. Witzenburger v. State ex rel. Wyoming
Community Development Authority, 575 P.2d 1100, 1127 (Wyo. 1978). Debt in excess of the
current year's taxes may only be created if approved by the state electorate.
The Wyoming Supreme Court has reviewed the constitutionality of a number of public financing
plans, but it has not reviewed a lease revenue financing plan like that authorized by HB0054. This
office cannot therefore predict with absolute certainty whether or not the Wyoming Supreme Court
would find that lease revenue financing creates state debt, in violation of Article 16, § 2. The Supreme
Court's prior decisions do, however, set forth a number of factors to consider in determining the
constitutionality of public financing plans. This office has reviewed those factors and numerous court
decisions from other jurisdictions addressing lease revenue financing, and, based upon that review, this
office concludes that lease revenue financing does not create debt in violation of Wyoming's
constitutional debt limitations.
Two Wyoming cases are of particular importance in determining the constitutionality of lease
revenue financing: Witzenburger v. State ex rel. Wyoming Community Development Authority,
575 P.2d 1100, 1127 (Wyo. 1978) and Laramie Citizens for Good Government v. City of
Laramie, 617 P.2d 474 (Wyo. 1980). In Witzenburger, the Wyoming Supreme Court reviewed the
Wyoming Community Development Act, the legislature's attempt through that act to create an entity
separate from the state to incur debt, and the obligations incurred by the state through the Act's various
provisions. In Laramie, the Court reviewed a purported lease-purchase agreement between the city of
28

Laramie and a private entity. The Court found the Witzenburger and Laramie financing arrangements
unconstitutional, but in so concluding, the Court did not hold that the state, or other governmental entity,
could never enter into a lease arrangement with a private entity, or that the state could not create a
private entity for that purpose; the Court simply outlined certain rules that must be followed in
structuring the arrangement to avoid violation of Wyoming's constitutional debt limitations. The
Witzenburger and Laramie financing plans did not comply with the rules, and as a result, public debt
was created in violation of Wyoming's constitutional debt limitations.
A. Witzenburger,
InWitzenburger, the Court concluded that the Wyoming Community Development Act
committed future state tax dollars to the repayment of bonds issued by the Wyoming Community
Development Authority, and therefore the Act created state debt. The Court found the commitment of
future state tax dollars through an indirect routing of state tax dollars to repay the community
development bonds and through the state's moral obligation to repay the bonds.
1. Indirect commitment of state tax dollars
In Witzenburger, the Court reviewed the Wyoming Community Development Act in
conjunction with the provisions of companion acts and found in that combination an indirect
commitment of future state tax dollars. The Court traced the route of state tax dollars as follows:
• Under the Wyoming Community Development Act, the Wyoming Community
Development Authority was authorized to issue bonds and to use its bond
proceeds to make loans to entities such as counties, municipalities, special
districts, joint power agencies and the State Highway Commission.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1107-08.
• Under a separate act, the state imposed a coal excise tax, with part of the proceeds to
be appropriated to the Wyoming Farm Loan Board. Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at
1107-08.
• The Wyoming Farm Loan Board was then authorized to grant coal excise tax revenues
to the same entities which received loans from the Authority. These entities could, and
did, in turn, with the approval of the Farm Loan Board, pledge the coal excise tax
revenues and future revenues for payment of their obligations to the Authority.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1109.
The Court reviewed three particular loans the Wyoming Community Development Authority
had made with its bond proceeds and found that Farm Loan Board grants of coal excise tax revenues
had been committed for the repayment of those loans. The excise taxes had been committed for
periods of five, fifteen and twenty years. The Court observed:
29

The Wyoming Community Development Authority Act and the
other legislation, companion to it, launches the state on a bold course of
public financing, drawing heavily on the name of the State of Wyoming,
subtly suggesting bonds are backed by an "obligation" of the State and
in the case of grants by the farm loan board, there is explicit, less subtle,
authority to make grants "* * * of the revenues derived or to be
derived from the excise tax levied" * * * Those grants (moneys derived
or to be derived from the excise tax), of course, may by the same
[provisions] be pledged "for the payment of any obligation to the
Wyoming community development authority, or other obligee, * * *."
By circuitous routing, tax money becomes funds committed to
secure and liquidate over a period of years bonds sold to the
public.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1116 (citations omitted and emphasis added).
The Court criticized the Wyoming Community Development Act as a "manipulation of public
tax money," and it concluded:
future tax money is offered as security for and payment of revenue
bonds, though reached in a round-about way: taxpayer to state
treasury, to farm loan board, to county, city, town, sewer district,
political subdivision or highway department, to Authority. The
legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly. Our
constitutional provisions, §§ 1 and 2, Article XVI, are explicit in their
checks that the prohibited indebtedness not be created "in any manner."
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1117 (emphasis added).
The Court found that the problem created by the commitment of these tax dollars was
compounded by the following pledge by the legislature, contained in the Wyoming Community
Development Act:
The state pledges to and agrees with the holders of any bonds
issued under this act (§§ 9-826 to 9-848), that the state will not limit or
alter the rights hereby vested in the authority to fulfill the terms of any
agreements made with the holders thereof, or in any way impair the
rights and remedies of such holders until such bonds together with the
interest thereon, with interest on any unpaid installments of interest, and
all costs and expenses in connection with any action proceeding by or
on behalf of such holders are fully met and discharged. The authority is
30

authorized to include this pledge and agreement of the state in any
agreement with the holders of such bonds.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1119 (quoting WYO. STAT. § 9-843). Concerning this pledge, the Court
stated:
By this clear commitment, the legislature has obligated itself for
the State that the legislature will not in any way alter or amend § 39-
227.10(d) and (e), which authorizes the farm loan board to make
grants of such "revenues derived or to be derived from the excise tax
levied" and authorizing the recipient of such go revenues or a pledge of
future revenues * * * (to) pledge wholly or in part, for the payment of
any obligation to the Wyoming community development authority, or
any other obligee, the monies derived or to be derived from the excise
tax, * * *. “ The State thus placed its faith and credit on the line,
and is irreversibly committed to a long-time discharge of debt, and
future legislatures cannot repeal the tax or divert it to other
purposes, once granted by the farm loan board.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1119-20.
Because of this long-term commitment of state tax dollars, albeit through an indirect routing, the
Court found the Wyoming Community Development Act created state debt and was therefore
unconstitutional.
2. Moral Obligation
In addition to the indirect commitment of future state tax dollars, the Court in Witzenburger
found that the Wyoming Community Development Act created a "moral obligation" on the part of the
state to guarantee payment of the bonds issued by the Wyoming Community Development Authority.
The Court defined a moral obligation as one that
arises out of a state of facts appealing to a universal sense of justice and
fairness, even though upon such facts no legally enforceable claim can
be based. * * * It is an obligation which, though lacking any foundation
cognizable in law, springs from a sense of justice and equity which an
honorable person would entertain, but not from a mere sense of doing
benevolence or charity.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1129.
31

Applying this definition of moral obligation, the Court found the following provision of the Act
morally obligated the state to repay the bonds issued by the Wyoming Community Development
Authority:
To assure the continued operation and solvency of the authority
for carrying out the public purposes of this act (§§ 9-826 to 9-848),
there may be appropriated, at the discretion of the legislature, and paid
to the authority for deposit in each debt service reserve fund such sum,
if any, as shall be certified by the chairman of the authority to the
governor as necessary to restore such fund or funds to an amount equal
to the maximum amount of principal and interest maturing and becoming
due in the next succeeding year on the bonds of the authority then
outstanding and secured by such fund or funds. The chairman of the
authority shall annually, on or before August 31 in each year, make and
deliver to the governor his certificate stating the sum, if any, required to
restore each such fund to the amount aforesaid, and the sum or sums so
certified, if any, may, at the discretion of the legislature, be appropriated
and paid to the authority during the then current state fiscal year.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1127.
The Court found this provision created a moral obligation because it was a representation to the
bondholders that would cause the bondholders to believe that the legislature's obligation to appropriate
funds to guarantee the bonds was not a discretionary one. Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1128. The
Court found that fair treatment of the bondholders morally obligated the state to repay the community
development bonds. The Court observed:
The provisions of the Act, creating what is referred to as a
"moral obligation" are misleading to those of the public who would
invest their money. If they were not intended as an attraction, a sales
gimmick, and if they had no significance, there would be no reason for
their existence as a part of the Act. We question the ethics of a
government utilizing such a merchandising technique. Principles of
justice and honesty fundamentally apply to individuals, municipalities,
states and the Nation alike, and should be applied alike.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1129 (citations omitted).
32

3. Witzenburger Requirements.
In Witzenburger, the Wyoming Supreme Court found the bonds issued pursuant to the
Wyoming Community Development Act unconstitutional because future state tax dollars were
committed to repay the bonds. The Court found that commitment in 1) the circuitous (indirect) routing
of state tax dollars, and 2) the moral obligation of the state to repay the bonds. The questions which
must be answered, in light of the Court's Witzenburger decision, with respect to the lease revenue
financing, is whether the state is directly or indirectly committing future state tax dollars and whether the
state is morally obligated to use future tax dollars to pay a debt created by the lease.
The answer to the first question, whether the lease revenue financing directly or indirectly
commits future tax dollars, is no. In Witzenburger, it was the circuitous routing of state tax dollars that
the Court found impermissible when it cautioned that the state cannot do indirectly what it cannot do
directly; it was not the attempted creation of an entity separate from the state (the Authority) which the
Court disallowed. In fact, the Court specifically stated:
We have little question but what the state legislature could
create a body corporate separate and distinct from that of the state as
asserted by the Authority and create obligations that are not those of
the state.
Witzenburger, 575 P.2d at 1115.
Additionally, the majority of courts which have reviewed lease revenue financing have found
that it does not, either directly or indirectly, create public debt1. The Wisconsin Supreme Court

1965); In re Opinion of the Justices No. 100, 41 So.2d 761 (Alabama 1949);

City of San Diego v. Rider, 55 Cal.Rptr.2d 422 (Cal. 1996); Gude v. City of

Good Government v. City of Laramie, 617 P.2d 474 (Wyo. 1980).
B. Laramie Citizens for Good Government v. City of Laramie
In Laramie, the Wyoming Supreme Court reviewed a financing structure used by the City of
Laramie to purchase a privately owned ranch to obtain needed water resources. Laramie, 617 P.2d at
474. The City of Laramie set up the following financing structure:
• a nonprofit corporation was created with the stated purpose to "promote, assist and
extend financial support to effect the desired and necessary facilities and improvements
throughout the City of Laramie, Wyoming, and owned or to be owned by the city;"
• the nonprofit corporation consisted of eleven members, nine of which were the city's
mayor and eight Laramie city council members;
• the nonprofit corporation was to issue bonds and use the proceeds to purchase the
private ranch. The bonds were to be serviced over fifteen years;
• the nonprofit corporation was to lease the ranch to the City of Laramie for fifteen years.
The city's annual rental payments were gauged by the bond debt service amount, and
the city was required to pay all taxes and assessments and construction and operating
expenses;
36

• at the end of the fifteen years, title to the ranch would be transferred to the city.
Laramie, 617 P.2d at 476-77.
The Supreme Court found that the city's lease of the ranch from the nonprofit corporation
created a debt in violation of constitutional debt limitations. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 479-80. The Court
also found that the bonds issued by the nonprofit corporation violated statutory bonding restrictions
applicable to municipalities. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 480-82. The lease of the ranch property created
city debt because the lease was not truly a lease, but was instead an installment sale and purchase
contract with an immediate obligation to pay the full purchase price. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 476-77.
The nonprofit corporation's bonds were subject to the city's statutory bonding restrictions because the
Court concluded the corporation was not an entity separate from the city, but was instead the alter ego
of the city. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 480-82. Each of the Court's conclusions will be separately
discussed below.
1. Lease v. Purchase Agreement
In concluding the City of Laramie's purported lease was not a lease, the Court identified a
number of factors to consider in determining whether an agreement is a lease or an installment
purchase contract. Factors indicating a lease include:
• a provision for cancellation of the lease by the lessee at its option at yearly intervals, or
the converse provision that the term is for one year with yearly renewal options;
• provision for payment of a fixed and substantial amount at the end of the lease term, or
the converse that there is no provision for transfer of title at the end of the term without
payment at that time of a fixed and substantial amount in addition to rental payments;
and
• provision that the lessor pay the cost of upkeep, repair, taxes, etc.
Laramie, 617 P.2d at 479-80.
In Laramie, the Court found that a review of these factors revealed the city of Laramie's
agreement with the corporation to be a purchase installment contract and not a lease. The agreement
required the city to pay semiannual installments for a fifteen year period, and it provided for title to pass
to the city with no additional amount to be paid at the end of the fifteen year period. Additionally, the
city could not terminate the agreement at the yearly intervals, and the city was required to pay all
property taxes, assessments, construction and operating expenses. Because the agreement was a
purchase agreement and not a lease, it represented an immediate obligation on the part of the city to
pay the entire purchase price and was therefore a debt. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 479-80.
37

2. Alter Ego
After first considering whether the city's lease of the ranch property created unconstitutional
debt, the Court next considered whether the bonds issued by the corporation created city debt in
violation of constitutional or statutory restrictions. The Court first found that the corporation was an
alter ego of the city and that legal limitations applicable to the city were therefore applicable to the
corporation. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 480. The Court concluded the bonds did not create debt in
violation of the applicable constitutional provisions, because the bonds were payable solely from
revenue created by the sale of the water, and not from future tax dollars. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 480.
Although the bonds did not violate constitutional debt limitations, the bonds, being an obligation of the
city, did violate statutory restrictions applicable to city bonds. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 481.
The Court's review of the bonds in Laramie is relevant to this discussion because of the Court's
ruling regarding the alter ego status of the nonprofit corporation. The Court held that, if a private entity
is the alter ego of the governmental entity, the debt limitations applicable to the governmental entity also
apply to the private entity. The Court did not, however, discuss in great detail the factors to consider in
determining whether a private entity is the alter ego of the governmental entity. One factor the Court
seemed to consider was the membership of the private entity--in Laramie, the nonprofit corporation's
membership was made up almost exclusively of the city's governing officials. Laramie, 617 P.2d at
482. The Court also considered the nature of the agreement between the private and governmental
entities. In Laramie, the city was obligated to make payments to the nonprofit corporation for a period
of fifteen years, which was also the debt service period for the corporation's bonds. The "lease"
payments over the fifteen years totaled the amount necessary to pay off the outstanding bonds.
Because the city was obligated for the entire debt service period and the nonprofit corporation had no
separate economic base, the two entities looked very much like one. Laramie, 617 P.2d at 482.
3. Laramie Requirements
In reviewing the constitutionality of the HBOO54 authorized lease revenue financing, two
questions must be answered under the Laramie analysis. First, is the lease truly a lease? And second,
is the nonprofit corporation from which the state will lease the prison facilities an entity separate from
the state, or is it the state's alter ego?
In answer to the first question, the state's lease of the prison facilities from the Wyoming Building
Corporation is truly a lease and not an investment purchase agreement. This is evidenced by the
following:
• unlike in the Laramie case, the state's lease of the prison facilities contains a
nonappropriation clause, allowing the state to terminate the lease should the legislature
fail to appropriate funds for the lease payments;
38

• the lease is for a period shorter than the debt service period, and the state's option to
purchase the prison facilities requires payment of a substantial sum at the end of the
lease term (approximately two times the annual lease payment);
• the Wyoming Building Corporation is required, under the terms of the lease, to pay: all
taxes, assessments or other charges lawfully imposed by any governmental body; all
gas, water, steam, electrical, heat, power and other utility charges; casualty and
property damage insurance; and public liability insurance.
The state's lease of the prison facilities is distinguishable in almost every respect from the "lease"
reviewed by the Wyoming Supreme Court in Laramie, and this office concludes that the state's lease of
the prison facilities is truly a lease and not an instrument purchase contract.
The second question, under the Laramie analysis, is whether the Wyoming Building
Corporation is an alter ego of the state. This office concludes that the answer to this question is no.
First, HB0054 authorizes the State Building Commission to approve the Wyoming Building
Corporation's formation, but the Wyoming Building Corporation is not a statutorily created state entity.
The Wyoming Building Corporation is a nonprofit corporation formed pursuant to the Wyoming
Nonprofit Corporation Act, WYO. STAT. § 17-19-101 et seq. Second, although the State Building
Commission must approve the membership of the Corporation's board of directors, the board is self-
perpetuating. New directors are elected by the directors then in office, subject again to the approval of
the State Building Commission. The State Building Commission does not appoint or remove members
of the board of directors, and the board of directors of the Wyoming Building Corporation will not
consist of State Building Commission members or otherwise mirror the state's governmental body.
A final consideration evidencing the separation between the state and the Wyoming Building
Corporation is the disparity of the obligations of each entity. The Wyoming Building Corporation is the
entity which issues bonds, and it is the sole entity obligated to repay those bonds over a twenty year
period. The state's only obligation is to make annual rental payments for a nineteen year period, subject
to annual appropriation by the legislature. The state's annual rental payments are not gauged by the
debt service amount, and if the legislature does not appropriate the funds to make the annual lease
payments, the state can terminate the lease, and the state's obligation will end at that time. The
Wyoming Building Corporation's obligation on the bonds will continue beyond the state's termination of
the lease, and the bondholders' recourse is against the Wyoming Building Corporation. This disparity in
obligations indicates that the state and the Wyoming Building Corporation are separate entities.
Under the Laramie analysis, the HBOO54 authorized lease revenue financing is constitutional.
The lease between the state and the Wyoming Building Corporation is truly a lease, and the state and
the Wyoming Building Corporation are separate entities.
CONCLUSION
39

Under the proposed lease revenue financing of the prison construction the state is not legally
obligated to repay any bonds issued by the Wyoming Building Corporation; nor is it obligated to make
future lease payments to the Wyoming Building Corporation. The state's lease obligations are
contingent upon annual appropriations by the legislature, and the state may in future years terminate the
prison lease and make alternative arrangements for the housing of the state's inmates. As the Wisconsin
Supreme Court appropriately observed in its review of a lease revenue financing plan, the wisdom or
likelihood of such choices is not relevant to a determination of the plan's constitutionality:
The test established in our cases for indebtedness * * * is not
whether the [governmental entity] will probably pay or whether the
[governmental entity] would be foolish not to pay. The test is whether
the [governmental entity] is under an obligation to pay and the creditor
has a right to enforce payment against the [governmental entity] or its
assets. No indebtedness is created "where payments are to be made
solely at the government's option."
Dieck, 477 N.W.2d at 618 (citations omitted).
The majority of state courts that have reviewed lease revenue financing plans have concluded
that lease revenue financing does not create government debt and therefore does not implicate
constitutional debt limitations. Only a small minority of courts have decided otherwise, and nothing in
Wyoming case law suggests the Wyoming Supreme Court would accept this minority position. In fact,
the Court's reasoning in Witzenburger and Laramie suggests the Court would accept the majority rule.
In Witzenburger, the Court stated that it did not doubt that the state could create a separate corporate
entity to incur debt. In Laramie, the Court could have, but did not, declared lease revenue financing
unconstitutional. It instead distinguished the Laramie financing structure from true lease revenue
financing.
The HB0054 authorized lease revenue financing is true lease revenue financing. The Wyoming
Building Corporation is an entity separate from the state, the state is under no obligation to continue
annual rent payments to the Corporation or to repay any bonds issued by the Corporation, and the
bondholders have no right to enforce payment against the state or the state's assets. The HBOO54
authorized lease revenue financing does not create state debt in violation of Article 16, § 2 of the
Wyoming Constitution.

The questions you have presented concern the definition of the term "gift." The Act provides a

must be read as a whole and in conjunction with other statutes on the same subject matter. Parker,
845 P.2d at 1042.
In Wyoming, legislative history is not available to shed light on the legislature's intent in enacting
a particular statute, and it is therefore helpful to consider other states' pronouncements regarding their

avoid even the appearance of impropriety. See Wyoming Attorney General Opinion No. 97-004.
Assuming the Wyoming legislature enacted the Ethics and Disclosure Act with a similar intent, the Act

public confidence in the integrity of government. This means the term gift, as used in the Ethics and
