P.2d 1100, reh. den. 577 P.2d 1386 (1978). With these principles in mind we move forward with
our analysis by defining the pertinent terms of Art. 6, § 15.
The term "qualified elector" is defined at WYO. STAT. § 22-1-102(a)(x) in Wyoming’s

The term "qualified elector" includes every citizen of the United States

STAT. § 22-3-102. The addition of the words "actually and physically" to the "bona fide"

Therefore, to be registered one must first be a bona fide resident and this condition is again a

For definition of the term "military office" we draw from Title 19, Chapter 7 which deals with

STAT. § 9-3-203(a)(lx).
"Officer" is defined at WYO. STAT. § 19-7- 101 (a)(vii) and at WYO. STAT. § 19-7-104,
the statute provides that each "assistant adjutant general shall hold the rank of brigadier general and
shall possess the qualifications set forth in WYO. STAT. at § 19-7-103 , most notable of which is the
requirement that the appointee “[b]e a resident of the state of Wyoming" at § 103(a)(iv). This
provision specifically making residency a requirement was added in 1998, amending and rewriting
WYO. STAT. § 19-2-204. The statutory scheme in existence prior to the amendments which were
effective July 1, 1998, also supports the conclusion that an appointment to the position of assistant
adjutant general is an appointment to a “military office” as that term is used in WYO. CONST. ART.
6, § 15.
At WYO. STAT. § 19-7-1051 the positions of “senior assistant adjutant general" and “junior
assistant adjutant general" are first recognized in statutory language and place these officers in the
direct line of succession in the event of disability, death, or absence of the adjutant general. Given the
fact that the adjutant general has authoritative and crucial statutory duties as outlined in WYO. STAT.
§19-7-103(b), the assistant adjutant general is clearly a position in which is "reposed some portion of
the sovereign power of the state." Geraud, supra.
The next consideration must be whether these military officials are
"appointed." WYO. STAT. §19-9-301(a) in pertinent part provides that:
All officers of the national guard of Wyoming shall be appointed by the
governor of Wyoming as provided in national guard regulations except
such officers as may be commissioned by the governor in an honorary
status or in a state status without regard to their allocation or
qualification by the department of defense of the United States.
While officers obtain their rank and commission pursuant to federal statute or regulation, the
appointment of National Guard officers is an attribute of state sovereignty specifically held by the
states and an officer enjoys that privilege under the will of the sovereign state. Crenshaw v. United
States, 134 U.S. 99, 33 L. Ed 825, 10 S. Ct. 431 (1890). The position of assistant adjutant general,
however, is to be distinguished from rank and commission, the latter being determined by federal
statute and regulation.
47

CONCLUSION
With these things in mind we conclude that an appointment to the position of assistant adjutant
general in the military office of the adjutant general is an “appointment” to a "military office" and such
person must be a "qualified elector" under the provisions of the Wyoming Constitution Art. 6, § 15.
Appointment that is inconsistent with the Constitution would therefore be in violation of the
Constitution's requisites, and could be held void. Allen, et al. v. State Board of Equalization, 110
P. 2d 73 (Cal. 1941). On this point we note that courts have held that a course pursued in conflict
with the Constitution, and any resolution, order or decree issued in conformity with that course, is
void. State ex rel. Schneider v. Kennedy, 225 Kan. 13, 587 P.2d 844 (1978) citing, with
approval, State v. Nelson, 210 Kan. 439, 502 P.2d 841 (1972).

QUESTIONS:The following questions have been presented concerning the reduced room rates that
several capitol area motels offer legislators who stay for extended time periods during
legislative sessions:
1. Under the Ethics and Disclosure Act, WYO. STAT. 9-13-101, et
seq., is it lawful for a legislator to accept a reduced rate from a motel
for an extended stay?
2. If so, must other persons who are similarly situated and stay a similar
length of time (such as lobbyists) also be able to receive the same
reduced rate as legislators?
3. If a legislator does not stay in a motel offering reduced rates during the
legislative session, can he still accept the reduced legislative rate during
the interim between sessions when he is on official business?
ANSWER: These three questions are related and will be grouped together for discussion
below. In answer to all three questions, a Wyoming legislator may accept a
motel room at a reduced rate as long as the rate paid for the room is adequate
consideration for the room.
DISCUSSION
The Ethics and Disclosure Act prohibits a legislator from using his position for his private
benefit. WYO. STAT. § 9-13-103(a) (Supp. 1998). As used in the Act, "private benefit" means the
49

receipt of a gift as a result of holding an office or position. WYO. STAT. § 9-13-103(b) (Supp.
1998). The acceptance of a motel room at a reduced rate is therefore prohibited by the Act if the
motel room at the reduced rate fits the definition of a gift.
The Act defines a gift as "anything of value to the extent that consideration of equal or greater
value is not received." This definition requires two determinations: first, a determination whether the
benefit or item received is an item of value, and second, a determination of whether consideration of
equal or greater value was given for the item received.
The motel room at a reduced rate is an item of value. See WYO. STAT. § 9-13-
102(a)(i)(M)(II). The question is whether the rate that the legislator pays is adequate consideration for
the room. This is a question of fact whose answer will depend on a number of factors, such as, the
difference between the rates normally charged and the rates charged a legislator, whether the reduced
rate is offered to all legislators or just a single or particular legislator, the level of increased occupancy
the motel expects to achieve as a result of the reduced rates and the potential for the increased use of
other services offered by the motel such as restaurants or gift shops. For example, a motel operator
may offer rooms at a reduced rate to legislators realizing that by doing so the operator will increase its
occupancy for an extended period of time. The increased occupancy, along with the increased use of
the motel's other services and the increased business drawn to the motel by the legislators' stay there,
may, and probably would, more than make up for the reduced rate. Thus, although the rate the
legislator pays is a reduced rate, it is nonetheless adequate consideration for the room, and the receipt
of the room at a reduced rate is therefore not a gift as the Act defines that term.
This result is consistent with the intent of ethics legislation generally. As this office observed in
a previous opinion, legislation such as the Ethics and Disclosure Act is intended to increase public
confidence in the integrity of government by preventing legislators or other public officials from
misusing their offices or taking official actions to serve personal interests. See Attorney General
Opinion No. 97-004. Where the circumstances surrounding a transaction support a determination that
adequate consideration has been exchanged, these objectives are served and the transaction does not
offend the Act.
CONCLUSION
The Ethics and Disclosure Act does not prohibit a legislator from accepting a motel room at a
reduced rate as long as the rate paid for the room is adequate consideration for the room. The
determination whether adequate consideration was exchanged for the room is one that can be made
without regard to the rate charged other individuals who may participate in a legislative session. The
answer to the second question is therefore no, other participating individuals, such as lobbyists, need
not be offered the same reduced rate as legislators.

QUESTION: By prohibiting an elected official from supervising or managing a family member
employed in a public office or position, does WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) effectively
prohibit an elected official's family member from working in the office of the elected
official?
ANSWER: No.
DISCUSSION
The question that has been presented concerning WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) is whether its
prohibition is a narrow prohibition against an official's direct oversight of a family member, or a
broader prohibition against a more generalized type of oversight, such as the official's overall
management of the office and the possible effect of that management on the employed family member.
In answering this question, we must consider the plain language of WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104, giving
effect to all of its parts. See Parker Land & Cattle Co. v. Wyoming Game & Fish Com'n. 845
P.2d 1040, 1042 (Wyo. 1993).
WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104 (Supp. 1998) provides:
(a) No public official, public member or public employee
shall advocate or cause the employment, appointment, promotion,
transfer or advancement of a family member to an office or position of
51

the state, a county, municipality or school district. A public official,
public member or public employee shall not supervise or manage a
family member who is in an office or position of the state, a county,
municipality or school district. (Emphasis added)
(b) A public official, public member or public employee,
acting in his official capacity, shall not participate in his official
responsibility or capacity regarding a matter relating to the employment
or discipline of a family member.
Whether the prohibition of WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104 is narrow or broad depends upon the
meaning given the terms "supervise" and "manage." Neither term is defined within the Ethics and
Disclosure Act, and we therefore give the terms their ordinary meaning.
The term supervise means "to superintend, oversee." Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary
1162 (1980). To superintend means "to have or exercise the charge and oversight of: direct," Id. at
1160, and to oversee means to "survey, watch." Id. at 812. The term oversight means “watchful and
responsible care," or "a careful watching." Id. at 812. It is apparent from these definitions that the term
supervise contemplates direct oversight of or control over the family member's work or duties.
The same is true of the definition of the term manage. To manage means "to direct or carry on
business or affairs.” Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary 691 (1980). In the context of WYO.
STAT. § 9-13-104(a), then, to manage a family member means to direct the member's business or
affairs, or to direct the member's work or duties.
The plain meaning of the terms supervise and manage, both of which contemplate direct
control or oversight, narrows the WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) prohibition. The prohibition extends
only to the elected official's direct supervision of a family member and does not necessarily prohibit a
family member from working in the office of an elected official.
This reading of WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) is consistent with WYO. STAT. § 9-13-
104(b)'s prohibition against an elected official acting directly or through others to approve, disapprove
or otherwise participate in the employment or discipline of a family member. See WYO. STAT. § 9-
13-104(b) in conjunction with WYO. STAT. § 9-13-102(a)(x). If WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a)
prohibited entirely a family member from working in the office or other domain of an elected official,
the occasion for the official to participate directly in the employment or discipline of a family member
could not arise. The WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(b) prohibition would therefore be unnecessary. To
give both §§ 104(a) and 104(b) effect, we must interpret the § 104(a) prohibition as a narrow one
prohibiting direct supervision or management of a family member's work.
CONCLUSION
52

WYO. STAT. § 9-13-104(a) prohibits an elected official from exercising direct supervisory
authority over a family member working in the official's office. It does not necessarily prohibit an
elected official's family member from working in the official's office. The prohibition against exercising
direct supervisory authority over a family member is of course in addition to the prohibition against
causing the employment, appointment, promotion, transfer or advancement of a family member to a
public office or position.
